Ecosystems and food chains:
An ecosystem is a community of living things (biotic factors) together with the nonliving parts of their surroundings (abiotic factors such as sunlight, water, soil and temperature). Producers make food by photosynthesis. Consumers eat other organisms: herbivores, carnivores and omnivores. Decomposers, such as fungi and bacteria, break down dead matter and return nutrients to the soil.

A food chain shows who eats whom, and arrows point in the direction energy flows. Many food chains join to form a food web. Only about 10% of energy passes from one level to the next, so there are fewer organisms at higher levels.
Relationships between living things:
Organisms in an ecosystem interact. Predation: a predator hunts and kills prey. Competition: organisms use the same limited resource, such as food, water, light or space. Symbiosis is a close, long-term relationship between two different species.

There are three types of symbiosis. In mutualism both species benefit, for example bees and flowers. In commensalism one species benefits and the other is not affected. In parasitism one species (the parasite) benefits and the other (the host) is harmed, for example a tick on a dog.

These relationships keep the numbers of populations balanced.
Human impact on the environment:
Human activities change ecosystems. Population growth increases the demand for food, water, energy and land. Deforestation destroys habitats and reduces the carbon dioxide taken up by plants. Burning fossil fuels causes air pollution and adds greenhouse gases, which contribute to global warming.

Water and soil pollution come from waste, fertilizers, pesticides and oil spills. Overhunting and overfishing can push species toward extinction. Introduced species can harm native ones. Habitat loss is the main cause of falling biodiversity, which is the variety of life in an area.
Protecting nature:
Protecting nature means using resources wisely so that they last for future generations. This is called sustainable use. The three Rs are reduce, reuse and recycle.

Governments create protected areas such as national parks, wildlife refuges and biosphere reserves. Laws limit hunting, fishing and pollution. Other actions include planting trees, saving water and energy, using public transport, treating wastewater and using renewable energy such as solar and wind power.

Endangered species are protected by conservation programs and captive breeding. Education and the choices of each person are also important.
